prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part B048 configuration, and I have tested it against the chair's questions. The physical idea is Katori's: choose the wavelength at which the ground and clock states of a neutral atom are shifted equally by the trapping light, so that thousands of atoms can sit in a lattice in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no first-order Doppler or recoil broadening and no lattice light shift. This is a statement about atomic polarisabilities, which is why it is atomic physics and not only engineering. As I recall the chronology, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock come from Katori's group around 2003 to 2005, with a closely related proposal from the SYRTE group (Lemonde and colleagues) in the same period. Ye's group then turned it into the reference system: it measured the clock transition with very high resolution, showed that atom-atom interactions in the lattice can be understood and suppressed, and took the clock to the low 10^-18 level, where the measurements become a probe of many-body physics, gravity over a millimetre, and possible drifts of constants. Independent laboratories reproduce clocks at this level, which is the robustness a theorist asks for. The two-name credit is the cleanest one on the shortlist: one name for the concept and first realisation, one for the decisive precision and many-body demonstration.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, the claim of Lemonde and of Takamoto, Ludlow and the Yb and Hg groups, and the fact that a clock is an instrument. I do not think the first is fatal, because the lattice clock needs an idea that neither the comb nor ion control supplies. But a colleague who insists on a new phenomenon will find the discovery content in the many-body physics inside the clock and in the tests of gravity and constants, and these are still in progress. On credit, two names will leave out people who contributed, and I cannot prove from memory that Katori and Ye are the only defensible pair. I am recalling priority dates and accuracy records and have not checked them against primary papers, and the chair is right that this should be said before we vote. The risk on the other side is also real: if the committee waits for the redefinition of the second, the field grows and credit becomes harder to assign.

responses.point: Holds B025 (atom interferometry) as the first alternative and does not propose it as a second prize part, because priority among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu is less settled than for Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I accept your reasoning and I move to the same place. In round 1 I called B025 a strong second; having counted names again, a second part would make five people against our limit of three, and I would not drop Chu or one of the clock pair to make it fit. Chu's light-pulse gravimeter and gyroscope were as decisive as Kasevich's later precision work, and the earlier laser-cooling and BEC prizes make the 'what is new' question harder than for the clock. I therefore treat B025 only as an alternative. If the committee ever returns to it, I think the credit would need to be thought through again, and I would not guess it now.

responses.point: Raises the possibility of a two-part prize combining B048 with another achievement, and asks the atomic-physics members to agree on Katori's priority and on the role of Ye's group.
responses.response: On the second part, I do not think one is needed. Any pairing with B048 must fit three names in total, which leaves a single extra person, and none of the shortlisted candidates has a credit set that small that I could defend. B033 (Halzen and Karle) and B052 each need two or three names, and the IceCube and EHT credit problems you described are exactly the kind I am not qualified to settle. On your priority question, speaking as the atomic-physics member: Katori's engineered-light-shift proposal and the first strontium lattice clock are his, and Ye's group provided the sustained accuracy, the interaction physics and the record comparisons. I would defend both names with that split, but I would check the 2003 to 2006 papers against the dates I am carrying in memory before the final ballot.

responses.point: Asks for a check of Katori's priority against the 2003 to 2005 papers, because the record favours Katori on priority, and wants to know if the ion-versus-lattice credit division is acceptable.
responses.response: I agree that the priority should be tested, and I am willing to do it as the member closest to this literature. My recollection is that the magic-wavelength proposal appeared in 2003 from Katori's group, the Lemonde group published a Sr lattice proposal around the same time with a somewhat different emphasis, and Katori's group made the first lattice-clock measurement in 2005. That favours Katori on priority and does not remove the need for Ye, whose group gave the demonstration of control and the 10^-18 era. It also answers your ion-versus-lattice question: ion clocks reach their accuracy by isolating one quantum system, while the lattice clock reaches it by averaging over many, which is a different resource and a different set of systematic effects. I would credit the lattice idea and not the ions.

responses.point: Judges that the redefinition of the second should not delay a prize and would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about how the credit is split between them. Also lists KPZ (B011) as unlikely this year.
responses.response: I agree on the pair, and I share your view that the exact split matters less than keeping both. For timing, I hold that waiting does not improve the scientific case: the discovery and its confirmation by independent laboratories are in hand, and the redefinition is a consequence and not a test. On KPZ, thank you for saying you now consider it unlikely. That was my worry in round 1: the credit would leave out Parisi and the exact-solution authors, and a one-member opening first place was not enough for me to move there. I would still like to see the universality class named in a future prize, but I cannot support it as this year's configuration.

responses.point: Adds that a purist could deny that the lattice clock is a new physical discovery, and notes that his own favourite B019 has an open credit problem (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore).
responses.response: I take the purist's challenge seriously, and I would answer it in the citation and not only in discussion. A citation about the lattice clock and its 10^-18 level makes clear that this is a new regime in which nature is probed, not just a better ruler. I also agree that your B019 concern is real. I considered B019 myself and placed it low in the opening, because the credit questions you describe (the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane and Mele, with Moore and Balents) would be hard for any trio to answer. I defer to you on condensed-matter priority, so if you think Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible set, I would like to hear which of those other claims you think are weakest.

responses.point: Gives up his EHT first choice for B048, and notes that Katori and Ye have collaborated and competed in ways he cannot adjudicate from the supplied text, and that the pending redefinition is open.
responses.response: I appreciate that you set aside your own first choice, and I do not think the EHT is less striking; it is a different kind of result, with a credit problem and a model-dependent gravity test that I cannot judge. On Katori and Ye, I would not read their collaboration and competition as a weakness. In experimental fields where two groups push one idea, that is how the confirmation arises. That the two groups agree to this accuracy makes the case stronger for me, since neither result stands alone. On the redefinition, I see it as a use of lattice clocks and not a reason to wait.

uncertainties: Exact priority dates for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 measurements are from memory; the whole committee, including me, has not checked primary papers.
Whether Lemonde and, to a lesser extent, Takamoto or Ludlow have a claim strong enough to join or displace Katori or Ye. I do not think so, but I cannot prove it from this table.
Whether the committee reads a measurement-capability achievement as a physics discovery, and how much weight the 2005 and 2012 prizes should carry.
Timing relative to the redefinition of the second: I would not wait, but I cannot exclude that others see it as part of the maturity argument.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B048 (Katori, Ye) or for B025 and B021. For transparency I repeat that I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller (ETH) groups; none of them is credited in any shortlisted candidate, and I see no need for recusal. I have no joint work with Katori or Ye, and I note that I have collaborated on theory with groups in the same field, which I treat as disclosure and not as a tie.
